newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: ZIMBABWE'S FMB MERGES WITH HERITAGE BANK.
newsitem.headline: ZIMBABWE'S FMB MERGES WITH HERITAGE BANK.

text.p: Zimbabwe's oldest merchant bank, the First Merchant Bank (FMB), has signed an agreement to merge with Heritage Investment Bank which was set up four years ago by local pension funds and some black businessmen.
FMB Holdings chairman David Dennett said that under the agreement, 2.4 million FMB shares would be issued to Heritage giving it a 10.5 percent stake in FMB.

In addition Anglo American Corporation Zimbabwe Ltd (AMZIM), the majority shareholder in FMB Holdings, had concluded a separate deal with Heritage giving the bank an 18-month option to acquire an additional 6.5 million shares in FMB.

This would increase Heritage's shareholding in FMB to 38.9 percent, making it the largest stakeholder in FMB and reducing Anglo's stake to 10 percent -- effectively localising the majority of the FMB shareholding.

Dennett told reporters that FMB had decided to merge with Heritage to ensure it remained a leading player in financial markets as competition intensified with a number of new banks coming onto the scene.
"As a consequence of increasing competition margins have declined and will continue to decline whereas costs have continued to escalate...," he said.

"As new banks continue to be registered it becomes more and more apparent that there will be a rationalisation in the market. FMB has for some time been studying developments in order to determine the most appropriate strategy to ensure it remains a leading player into the 21st century," he said.
Dennett said the merger would strengthen FMB's position in treasury and corporate finance activities and also produce a stronger skills base.

The merged bank will still be known as First Merchant Bank Zimbabwe, and FMB's current managing director Ray Feltoe has been appointed its chief executive. Heritage's managing director Douglas Munatsi maintains that position in the new venture.

Meanwhile, Anglo chief executive Phillip Baum dismissed suggestions that his corporation had scaled down its stake in FMB under pressure from President Robert Mugabe's government to localise some of its activities.
"There's been absolutely no political pressure to do so. It was a straightforward commercial process. We are happy to have our minority shareholding in the new entity," Baum told reporters.
He said the proceeds from the sale of part of its shareholding in FMB to Heritage, estimated at about Z$300 million, would be reinvested in its local activities.

"This money, such as we realise from it, it's not about disinvesting from Zimbabwe but investing in our more traditional activities... We are confident about the Zimbabwean economy and we would like to do a lot of things here," he said.
